verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's medical malpractice laws are governed primarily by statutes that set rules for damage caps (S.C. Code § 15-32-220), pre-suit filing and mandatory mediation (S.C. Code § 15-79-125), and expert affidavits (S.C. Code § 15-36-100).
verifiedClaims.note: Verified 2026-10-05 against scstatehouse.gov chapters 32, 36, 79.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. South Carolina imposes a cap on non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases under S.C. Code § 15-32-220. The current caps are:
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-32-220(E): the noneconomic limits 'do not apply if the jury or court determines that the defendant was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton, or reckless, and such conduct was the proximate cause of the claimant's noneconomic damages, or if the defendant has engaged in fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or if the defendant altered or destroyed medical records with the purpose of avoiding a claim or liability to the claimant.' Intoxication is NOT a § 15-32-220 exception (it lifts the punitive cap under § 15-32-530(C)(3)).
verifiedClaims.note: The post never states the (E) exceptions — the most important cap fact on a 'damage caps' post. Add after the table (or after 'The current caps are:' paragraph): 'The caps do not apply if the provider was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, committed fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or altered or destroyed medical records to avoid liability (S.C. Code § 15-32-220(E)).' Also note the caps are 'for each claimant' and apply 'when final judgment is rendered' (A)-(C).

verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA memo 'Non-Economic (Medical Malpractice) Damages Limitation – Inflation Component', 2026-02-03 (read from the PDF 2026-10-05): CPI-U up 70.3% from 190.3 (Dec 2004) to 324.054 (Dec 2025); 'the limit against a single health care provider and a health care institution for each claimant ... when final judgment is rendered increases to $596,001. Also, the limit against all health care providers and all health care institutions for each claimant ... increases to $1,788,002.' Effective on publication in the State Register (§ 15-32-220(F)). Base: 'three hundred fifty thousand dollars for each claimant' (§ 15-32-220(A)).
verifiedClaims.note: Table row; both figures verified. Base figure is labelled as indexed — not stale.

verifiedClaims.claim: These caps apply only to non-economic damages — pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, and similar quality-of-life losses. There is no cap on economic damages such as medical bills, lost wages, and lost earning capacity.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-32-220(D)(1): 'The provisions of this section do not limit the amount of compensation for economic damages suffered by each claimant in a medical malpractice claim.' (D)(2): nor punitive damages.

verifiedClaims.claim: If your malpractice injury required $2 million in corrective surgery and ongoing care, you can recover the full amount of those economic losses.
verifiedClaims.note: Illustrative hypothetical, consistent with (D)(1). Optional: 'if proven'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also caps punitive damages at three times the compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA memo 'Punitive Damage Award Limitation – Inflation Component', 2026-02-03 (read from PDF): CPI-U up 47.8% from 219.179 (Dec 2010) to 324.054 (Dec 2025); 'the limit increases to $739,245.' § 15-32-530(A): greater of three times compensatory 'or the sum of five hundred thousand dollars' (indexed under (D)). Exceptions: (B) greater of four times or $2,000,000 where conduct was motivated primarily by unreasonable financial gain known/approved by management, or could subject the defendant to a felony conviction; (C) no cap where the defendant intended harm, pled guilty to/was convicted of a felony from the same conduct, or acted while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs. § 15-32-220(D)(2): the med-mal noneconomic cap does not limit punitive damages.
verifiedClaims.note: $739,245 verified. Unqualified 'caps' omits the (B)/(C) tiers. Minimal edit: append ', with higher limits or no cap for certain egregious conduct, such as intent to harm, felony conduct, or acting while impaired by alcohol or drugs'. Same in faq:0.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-32-520(D): 'Punitive damages may be awarded only if the plaintiff proves by clear and convincing evidence that his harm was the result of the defendant's wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct.' § 15-33-135: the plaintiff 'has the burden of proving such damages by clear and convincing evidence.'
verifiedClaims.note: Substance right; add the burden: '...was wilful, wanton, or reckless, proven by clear and convincing evidence (S.C. Code §§ 15-32-520, 15-33-135).' § 15-32-520 is at https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c032.php.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina imposes a three-year statute of limitations for medical malpractice claims under S.C. Code § 15-3-545. The clock generally starts on the date the treatment or negligent act occurred.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-545(A): 'within three years from the date of the treatment, omission, or operation giving rise to the cause of action or three years from date of discovery or when it reasonably ought to have been discovered, not to exceed six years from date of occurrence'. Public hospitals (MUSC is run by the Medical University Hospital Authority, 'an agency of the State of South Carolina', S.C. Code § 59-123-60(E); Tatum v. MUSC, 346 S.C. 194 (2001)) are sued under the S.C. Tort Claims Act, not § 15-32-220: sue the agency, not its employed doctors (§ 15-78-70); 'forever barred unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered' (three if a verified claim was first filed) (§ 15-78-110); $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence, or $1,200,000 where the loss was 'caused by the tort of any licensed physician or dentist, employed by a governmental entity' (§ 15-78-120(a)(1)-(4)); no punitive damages or prejudgment interest (§ 15-78-120(b)).
verifiedClaims.note: Three years and trigger verified. Add: 'Claims against MUSC or another public hospital fall under the S.C. Tort Claims Act, which generally allows two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110).' The post names MUSC as a defendant without mentioning this.

(B) also covers 'the negligent placement of any appliance or apparatus'; subsection (A) applies to 'actions other than actions controlled by subsection (B)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Before filing a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina, the plaintiff must file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and serve it on each defendant (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(A): 'shall contemporaneously file a Notice of Intent to File Suit and an affidavit of an expert witness, subject to the affidavit requirements established in Section 15-36-100, in a county in which venue would be proper'; notice 'must name all adverse parties as defendants' and 'must be served upon all named defendants in accordance with the service rules for a summons and complaint'.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim 2026-10-05.

verifiedClaims.claim: The expert's affidavit must specify at least one negligent act or omission.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(B): the affidavit 'must specify at least one negligent act or omission claimed to exist and the factual basis for each claim based on the available evidence at the time of the filing of the affidavit'. A defective affidavit can be cured 'by amendment within thirty days of service of the motion' alleging the defect (§ 15-36-100(E)); missing affidavit → 'subject to dismissal for failure to state a claim' ((C)(1)); not required where negligence is 'within the ambit of common knowledge and experience' ((C)(2)).
verifiedClaims.note: Add 'and the factual basis for each claim'. SC's 30-day cure is in (E) (SC's own rule, not imported from Georgia). Optional add: 'A defective affidavit can be cured by amendment within 30 days of a motion challenging it (S.C. Code § 15-36-100(E)).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing the notice tolls (pauses) the statute of limitations, so it does not consume your time to sue. The parties must then mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, and the lawsuit can be filed only if mediation fails.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 'Filing the Notice of Intent to File Suit tolls all applicable statutes of limitations' (§ 15-79-125(A)). 'Within ninety days and no later than one hundred twenty days from the service of the Notice of Intent to File Suit, the parties shall participate in a mediation conference unless an extension for no more than sixty days is granted by the court based upon a finding of good cause' ((C)). If mediation fails, suit must be filed 'within sixty days after the mediator determines that the mediation is not viable, that an impasse exists, or that the mediation should end; or prior to expiration of the statute of limitations, whichever is later' ((E)).
verifiedClaims.note: 'Generally' covers the 60-day extension. Recommended add (the post never gives the post-mediation deadline): 'If mediation fails, the lawsuit must be filed within 60 days after the mediator declares an impasse, or before the limitation period would otherwise expire, whichever is later (S.C. Code § 15-79-125(E)).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Your attorney needs time to obtain medical records and to find a qualified expert who will sign the affidavit before the notice can be filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Note § 15-79-125(B): after the notice is filed and served, the parties 'may subpoena medical records' and, with leave of court, take depositions.

verifiedClaims.claim: After the Notice of Intent is served, the parties must go through a mediation process, generally within 90 to 120 days, where a neutral third party attempts to facilitate a settlement between them.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(C); governed by the Circuit Court ADR Rules.

verifiedClaims.claim: If mediation is unsuccessful, the lawsuit can then be filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(E)(1)-(2): within 60 days after impasse or before the limitation period expires, whichever is later.
verifiedClaims.note: Add the deadline: '...can then be filed — within 60 days of the impasse or before the limitations period runs, whichever is later (S.C. Code § 15-79-125(E)).'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina medical malpractice claims require the plaintiff to prove four elements by a preponderance of the evidence:
verifiedClaims.note: Standard civil burden; four-element framework accepted in sibling packs.

verifiedClaims.claim: Expert testimony is required to establish both the standard of care and the breach. The expert must be a licensed healthcare professional in the same or similar specialty as the defendant.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(A): expert must be licensed 'to practice his or her profession in the location in which the expert practices or teaches' and EITHER (2)(a) board certified in the area of practice about which the opinion is offered OR (2)(b) actively practicing/teaching in it 'for at least three of the last five years immediately preceding the opinion'; OR (A)(3) a person with 'scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge'. No expert is needed for negligence 'within the ambit of common knowledge and experience' ((C)(2)).
verifiedClaims.note: 'same or similar specialty' is Georgia-style phrasing, not SC's test. Minimal edit: 'Expert testimony is generally required to establish the standard of care and the breach. The expert must be licensed in his or her profession and either board certified in the relevant area or have practiced or taught in it for at least three of the last five years (S.C. Code § 15-36-100).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Without qualified expert testimony, a medical malpractice case cannot survive summary judgment in South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Common-knowledge exception: § 15-36-100(C)(2) (no affidavit needed where negligence 'lies within the ambit of common knowledge and experience, so that no special learning is needed').
verifiedClaims.note: Absolute as written. Minimal edit: 'Without qualified expert testimony, most medical malpractice cases cannot survive summary judgment in South Carolina.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Economic damages (medical bills, lost wages) are uncapped.

South Carolina caps non-economic damages at a base of $350,000 per provider or institution and $1,050,000 in total per claimant, adjusted each year for inflation: for 2026, $596,001 and $1,788,002 (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA memo 'Non-Economic (Medical Malpractice) Damages Limitation – Inflation Component', 2026-02-03 (read from the PDF 2026-10-05): CPI-U up 70.3% from 190.3 (Dec 2004) to 324.054 (Dec 2025); 'the limit against a single health care provider and a health care institution for each claimant ... when final judgment is rendered increases to $596,001. Also, the limit against all health care providers and all health care institutions for each claimant ... increases to $1,788,002.' Effective on publication in the State Register (§ 15-32-220(F)). § 15-32-220(E): the noneconomic limits 'do not apply if the jury or court determines that the defendant was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton, or reckless, and such conduct was the proximate cause of the claimant's noneconomic damages, or if the defendant has engaged in fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or if the defendant altered or destroyed medical records with the purpose of avoiding a claim or liability to the claimant.' Intoxication is NOT a § 15-32-220 exception (it lifts the punitive cap under § 15-32-530(C)(3)).
verifiedClaims.note: All four figures correct and base figures are labelled as indexed. FAQPage structured data — add: 'The cap does not apply if the provider was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, committed fraud, or altered or destroyed records to avoid liability.' Public hospitals: Tort Claims Act caps instead.

verifiedClaims.claim: There is no cap on economic damages like medical bills and lost wages.
Punitive damages are capped at three times compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA punitive memo 2026-02-03: 'the limit increases to $739,245'. § 15-32-530(B): 4x / $2,000,000 tier; (C): no cap for intent to harm, felony plea/conviction, substantial impairment.
verifiedClaims.note: Figure verified. Append ', with higher limits or no cap for certain egregious conduct'. Structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina imposes a three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-545) from the date of the negligent act or from when the injury was or should have been discovered.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-545(A) verified ('when it reasonably ought to have been discovered'). Public hospitals: two years (§ 15-78-110).
verifiedClaims.note: Add '— two years if the claim is against MUSC or another public hospital (S.C. Code § 15-78-110)'. Optional: 'reasonably should have been'. Structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: A six-year statute of repose generally applies — in most cases no claim can be filed more than six years after the negligence occurred.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Generally' covers foreign objects.

verifiedClaims.claim: before filing a malpractice lawsuit you must file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit (S.C. Code § 15-36-100), and serve it on each defendant. Filing the notice tolls the statute of limitations. The parties must then mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, before the lawsuit can be filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(A),(C) verbatim (see body).
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Optional: the 60-day post-impasse filing window ((E)).

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. South Carolina requires mandatory mediation in medical malpractice cases before the lawsuit is filed (S.C. Code § 15-79-125). A neutral mediator attempts to facilitate a settlement. If mediation is unsuccessful, the lawsuit can then be filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(C): mediation within 90–120 days of service of the notice (60-day good-cause extension); (E): file within 60 days after impasse or before the limitation period expires, whichever is later.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate but lacks timing. Append: 'Mediation generally takes place 90 to 120 days after the notice is served; if it fails, suit must be filed within 60 days of the impasse or before the limitations period runs, whichever is later.' Structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's six-year statute of repose (S.C. Code § 15-3-545) generally bars a medical malpractice lawsuit filed more than six years after the negligent act, even if the injury was not discovered until later.
verifiedClaims.note: Optional: '(objects left in the body are an exception, § 15-3-545(B))'.

verifiedClaims.claim: This is more generous than Georgia's five-year repose period but still bars some legitimate claims.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71(b) five years is correct, but Georgia's repose has exceptions (§§ 9-3-72, 9-3-73) and the comparison is unsourced on an SC post.
verifiedClaims.note: GA mention 3 of 3, in FAQPage structured data. Drop the Georgia clause: 'It still bars some legitimate claims, so do not wait to have your records reviewed.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Hospitals, medical centers, individual physicians, nurses, specialists, pharmacies, and nursing homes can all be sued for medical malpractice in South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Public hospitals (MUSC is run by the Medical University Hospital Authority, 'an agency of the State of South Carolina', S.C. Code § 59-123-60(E); Tatum v. MUSC, 346 S.C. 194 (2001)) are sued under the S.C. Tort Claims Act, not § 15-32-220: sue the agency, not its employed doctors (§ 15-78-70); 'forever barred unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered' (three if a verified claim was first filed) (§ 15-78-110); $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence, or $1,200,000 where the loss was 'caused by the tort of any licensed physician or dentist, employed by a governmental entity' (§ 15-78-120(a)(1)-(4)); no punitive damages or prejudgment interest (§ 15-78-120(b)). Pharmacists are 'health care providers' and nursing homes 'health care institutions' under § 15-32-210(4)-(5).
verifiedClaims.note: Add the public-hospital rule: 'If the hospital is MUSC or another public hospital, the claim runs under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act: you sue the hospital rather than its employed doctors, within two years, with damages capped at $300,000 per person ($1.2 million for a government-employed physician or dentist) and no punitive damages (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-70, 15-78-110, 15-78-120).' Structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Each provider or institution is subject to its own non-economic damage cap ($596,001 for 2026), up to $1,788,002 in total for all defendants combined (S.C. Code § 15-32-220), which is why identifying all liable parties is critical to maximizing your total recovery.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA memo 'Non-Economic (Medical Malpractice) Damages Limitation – Inflation Component', 2026-02-03 (read from the PDF 2026-10-05): CPI-U up 70.3% from 190.3 (Dec 2004) to 324.054 (Dec 2025); 'the limit against a single health care provider and a health care institution for each claimant ... when final judgment is rendered increases to $596,001. Also, the limit against all health care providers and all health care institutions for each claimant ... increases to $1,788,002.' Effective on publication in the State Register (§ 15-32-220(F)).
verifiedClaims.note: Figures and mechanics verified (per claimant). Optional: 'all health care defendants combined' and 'unless an exception applies'.
